growth_story.headline: Hurricanes, two debt restructurings and tourism's swings shaped Grenada's growth; income per person has grown 2.8 percent a year since 2014, to a record high.
growth_story.arc: Grenada's income per person grew 1.2 percent a year in 1990–1997 and 5.3 percent in 1998–2005, a fast but uneven era in which the government borrowed heavily for capital projects. Hurricanes Ivan in 2004 and Emily in 2005 caused unprecedented damage, and the first of two debt restructurings ran from 2004 to 2006. From 2006 to 2013 growth averaged -0.7 percent: the global financial crisis hit tourism and construction before the economy had recovered from the storms, and public debt became unsustainable. After a second debt restructuring in 2013–15 and a new fiscal responsibility framework, growth averaged 2.8 percent over 2014–2025, led by tourism, construction and farming. That era also held the deepest fall in the record, 14.0 percent in 2020, when tourism collapsed and St George's University stopped in-person classes, but income per person recovered and reached its highest level yet in 2025.

threads.title: Hurricanes and a debt build-up
threads.text: In the early 2000s the government borrowed to pay for capital projects, and debt rose fast. Then two hurricanes, Ivan in 2004 and Emily in 2005, caused unprecedented damage, and a first debt restructuring followed in 2004–06. Income per person fell 1.0 percent in 2004, jumped 12.9 percent in 2005 and fell 4.3 percent in 2006.

threads.title: Global crisis and a second default
threads.text: The global financial crisis hit tourism and construction hard, and income per person fell 6.9 percent in 2009; it did not climb back above its 2008 level until 2015. Government spending meant to cushion the downturn left large fiscal gaps, and a second debt restructuring followed in 2013–15. The IMF credits a fiscal responsibility framework with restoring confidence and cutting public debt in the years of growth that followed.

threads.title: Pandemic and the university
threads.text: Income per person fell 14.0 percent in 2020, the largest drop in the record. Tourism collapsed and St George's University, a key part of local activity, stopped in-person classes. Growth came back at 4.4 percent in 2021 and 7.1 percent in 2022.

threads.title: Tourism, imports and storms
threads.text: Tourism remains the main engine, which leaves growth exposed to downturns abroad and to hurricanes. The IMF finds that the tourism-led model has done less than it could to lift the economy's lasting capacity, because many inputs are imported and local investment has been weak.

threads.title: Citizenship sales and foreign investment
threads.text: Money from selling citizenship and from foreign direct investment flows in on a large scale. In 2025 net foreign direct investment came to 13.5 percent of GDP while the current account deficit was 21.8 percent of GDP. The IMF credits careful saving of citizenship receipts with keeping public finances comfortable, and lists a halt in these inflows as a risk.

since_last_year.text: Income per person grew 4.3 percent in 2025, up from 2.3 percent in 2024, and reached a new high. The World Bank credits rebuilding after Hurricane Beryl, new hotel building and farming, while the number of overnight visitors fell. Citizenship receipts fell back from their recent highs, and the fiscal rule suspended after Beryl is due to return in 2027.

growth_story.tension: The World Bank describes a decade of strong growth that beat most Eastern Caribbean peers, but its average leaves out 2020 and counts the whole economy. With the 14.0 percent fall of 2020 included, income per person grew 2.1 percent a year over 2016–2025, ranking 8 of 11 among structural peers. An IMF paper describes a relatively robust growth trend for the whole economy in the decades after independence, while income per person grew only 1.2 percent a year in 1990–1997.
